items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.quote: the interests of the company's employees
items.why: Source of the quotation. Employees' interests are one of six matters directors must have regard to while promoting the company's success for the benefit of its members; the duty is owed to the company, not to employees, and does not prescribe an assessment or a record.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CZA: Section 172(1) statement
items.quote: describes how the directors have had regard to the matters set out in section 172(1)(a) to (f) when performing their duty under section 172
items.why: The reporting duty that makes the record matter: the strategic report must describe how directors had regard to the section 172 matters. It does not apply to a company that qualifies as medium-sized (and small companies do not prepare a strategic report). Inserted by the Companies (Miscellaneous Reporting) Regulations 2018 (S.I. 2018/860), per the textual note on the page.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 248: Minutes of directors' meetings
items.quote: Every company must cause minutes of all proceedings at meetings of its directors to be recorded.
items.why: The duty to minute. It requires a record of proceedings; it does not say what the minute must contain, so a record of the workforce assessment is good practice built on this duty, not a statutory requirement.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.quote: have been considered in board discussions and decision-making
items.why: Provision 5 asks the board to describe in the annual report how stakeholder views and the section 172 matters were considered in board discussions and decision-making, and to engage the workforce through a workforce director, an advisory panel or a designated non-executive. Applies on a comply-or-explain basis to listed companies; used by others as a benchmark.

items.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, section 188: Duty of employer to consult representatives
items.quote: The consultation shall begin in good time and in any event
items.why: The point at which a job-loss effect becomes a legal duty: collective consultation where 20 or more redundancies are proposed at one establishment within 90 days, with written disclosure of reasons and numbers. The page shows prospective amendments from the Employment Rights Act 2025 (a threshold across establishments) in brackets; whether they are in force was not established.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing
items.why: The nearest existing statutory assessment made before adoption: where workplace AI processes staff data at high risk, the assessment comes first and staff or their representatives are asked for their views where appropriate. It covers data protection risk, not job change.

items.title: 1 in 4 workers worry that AI will lead to job losses
items.locator: 'Some top tips for employers from Acas on the use of AI at work'
items.quote: If there is an expectation that certain roles begin using AI, that could mean a change of terms and conditions.
items.why: Acas advice that employers should have clear policies and consult employees and representatives on introducing AI, issued with a survey of 1,023 employees. Advice in a news release, not a statutory code.

items.title: Labour Market Outlook: Autumn 2025
items.locator: Key points (page 5) and section on artificial intelligence (page 16 onwards)
items.quote: Employees in three-quarters of UK organisations are using AI tools at work (76%).
items.why: Source of the figure: 17% of employers expect the use of AI tools to reduce their headcount in the next 12 months; survey of 2,019 UK employers by YouGov, fieldwork 19 September to 14 October 2025. The CIPD's press release says the 17% excludes employers who do not know whether AI tools are used (6% of the sample). Expectations, not outcomes.

items.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140)
items.quote: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure.
items.why: International comparator. Finds that transformation of jobs, not replacement, is the most likely effect, that exposure is higher for women and in high-income countries, and that the change should be managed through social dialogue. Exposure is a measure of tasks, not a forecast of job losses. No publication date is printed on the web edition; 2025 is taken from the text.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: deployers who are employers shall inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). A duty to inform before a high-risk system is used at work; it is not a duty to assess job impact. The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text shown is not yet updated; no application date is given in the brief.
